interactions.summary: Forese parts from Dante with a prophecy of ruin and punishment, the travelers pass another gluttony tree, and an angel opens the next ascent with a beatitude about just measure.
Jiang turns back to the student’s opening dream and asks whether the dream-tree and blocked river were already anticipating this purgatorial scene and a need for redemption.

claims.claim: Forese predicts that Dante’s city is being deprived of good and is headed toward wretched ruin, with Corso dragged to destruction.
The second gluttony tree repeats the pedagogy of denied fruit: longing is provoked and then disciplined by command and exempla.
Jiang explicitly links the student’s dream to the purgatory tree scene and frames the dream as a sign that the seminar is already working on the student’s conscience.
The student himself interprets the dream as bound up with change, reflection on past wrongs, and a desire for redemption.

signature_moments.moment: The poem catches up to the dream so closely that Jiang treats the dream as a live interpretive event inside the seminar.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the class itself part of the source’s metaphysical drama rather than just its audience.

signature_moments.moment: The student ties purgatory to an inventory of the wrongs he has done and a desire to seek redemption.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a way for me to seek redemption
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a performed example of the text converting literary discussion into self-judgment.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is important for June 26 because Jiang explicitly folds the class’s dream-life into the purgatory reading as evidence of seminar pressure.
